name: Hilda
summary:
Hilda of Whitby was a saint and the first abbess of the monastery at Whitby in 664, playing a pivotal role in the Christianisation of Anglo-Saxon England. She was born into a pagan family but converted to Christianity and became a key figure in the early Church in Britain.

The Synod of Whitby, convened by Hilda in 664, marked a significant turning point in the conversion of the Anglo-Saxons to Christianity. The synod resulted in the imposition of Roman Catholic practices on the Anglo-Saxon Church, leading to a lasting impact on British history and culture.

Hilda's legacy extends beyond her role as abbess, as she also served as a model for future generations of women in leadership positions within the Church. Her wisdom and influence were sought by kings and nobles, earning her a reputation as one of the most important figures in Anglo-Saxon England.

In 680, Hilda died on November 17, leaving behind a legacy that continues to shape British Christianity and culture today.
